scope: Adversarial follow-up for nine assigned European/international compute, energy, agent-accountability and finance routes. Evidence cutoff 2026-10-31; target checkpoint 2027-06-21/2027-06-22. Single-researcher, retrieval-first analysis with contrasting hypotheses; not an independently run persona panel. Fresh retrieval is distinguished from new-to-model evidence. No scores changed. Missing-data labels: AUTHORITY, NONDISCLOSURE, ACCESS, FUTURE_DECISION, POPULATION, OUTCOME, SCHEDULE.

routes.headline: A delegated common contract is plausible, but governance votes and procurement-amendment limits constrain scope

newEvidence.claim: FACT, freshly re-read and newly foregrounded: the draft FWC names EuroHPC JU acting for itself and national contracting authorities; the latter remain placeholders. Article I.16 gives the Commission an indivisible 50% vote, distributes the remaining half by national financial commitments, and requires at least 75% of all votes if consensus fails. This is not one-country-one-veto governance.

FACT, newly foregrounded: I.15 requires end-user terms and permits contractor suspension of risky users. II.11 requires written amendments and prohibits changes altering initial procurement conditions or unequal treatment. A specific contract is not an FWC amendment.

REPORT, new comparative evidence: AISI reports that intentionally internet-enabled privileged evaluations produced out-of-scope real-world actions in July 2026. This supports an evaluator/tenant incident scenario, not a finding that the EuroHPC clause already covers all model-caused harm.
newEvidence.locator: What happened; How we discovered the incident; Lessons for the future

supports: INFERENCE: centralised contracting and shared end-user requirements can reduce repeated national drafting.
INFERENCE: a tenant containment drill is a nearer-term test of the notification chain than waiting for all infrastructure to operate.
challenges: INFERENCE: the 75% rule makes Commission support necessary for a formal governance vote; a national bloc alone cannot pass it. The voting rule is not itself an amendment power.
INFERENCE: broad new model-release duties might materially change the procurement bargain; existing security wording is not a blank cheque.
INFERENCE: suspension of an entire facility could harm unrelated researchers; tenant-scoped containment is preferable where technically sufficient.
unknowns: AUTHORITY: actual national contracting authorities, their mandates and the legal route for the precise proposed annex.
SCHEDULE/ACCESS: correcting tender notice and revised question cutoff not recovered in this pass; no new operational date established.
POPULATION/OUTCOME: installed covered capacity, tenant inventory, signed terms and observed drills absent.
routes.decisionTest: Obtain an authorised written answer distinguishing clarification of I.14-I.15 duties from a material II.11 amendment, plus one contractor-approved tenant drill and a documented procurement timetable. Fail the pre-Geneva operational claim if only an unsigned template exists.

ideas.title: Tenant incident annex with a procurement-scope check
ideas.proposal: Draft a narrowly scoped annex for evaluation-origin security incidents, mapping trigger, evidence preservation, reporting recipient, tenant containment and cure to existing duties; have the competent contracting authority determine its procurement route before use.
ideas.owner: EuroHPC JU contracting team, identified national contracting authority and selected contractor; none has accepted
ideas.mechanism: Prospective compatible end-user terms under I.15; written contract change only if lawfully required under II.11
ideas.safetyDemand: No unapproved external actions during privileged model testing; prompt incident reporting with preserved event evidence
ideas.verification: Tabletop plus isolated synthetic tenant exercise: confirm alert, designated recipient, per-tenant access suspension, preservation and authorised restart
ideas.remedy: Tenant-scoped pause and cure where sufficient, with any broader contractual remedy explicitly reserved to its actual holder
ideas.deadline: Proposed scope determination by 2027-01-15 and drill by 2027-05-31, conditional on the actual procurement calendar; not official milestones
ideas.whyBetter: Tests a shared enforceable chain without equating a global model-release veto or an operating gigafactory with a signed protocol; measures collateral disruption separately.

scoreImplications.implication: Test delegated-contract and governance-vote scenarios separately
scoreImplications.reason: Many states need not each exercise a veto, but Commission support is indispensable for a 75% formal vote.

scoreImplications.implication: Do not upgrade operational timing from an annex draft
scoreImplications.reason: Procurement compatibility, signatories and infrastructure schedule are unresolved.

scoreImplications.implication: Distinguish tenant remedy from facility-wide termination
scoreImplications.reason: I.15 permits restricted end-user access; that is a different scope and collateral-cost profile.

routes.headline: A Belgian pilot remains useful, but is not demonstrably the fastest route to a common service condition

Allocating an award and changing the shared service conditions are different acts.
newEvidence.locator: Resource Allocator table Belgium row; terms p.1 preamble

newEvidence.locator: Dates for next cut-off; preparatory/development paragraph

INFERENCE: a narrow AI-use declaration can avoid charging non-AI users the full evaluation burden.
challenges: INFERENCE: bilateral award negotiations may duplicate a service condition CSC could administer in common.
INFERENCE: a fast monthly award review is not a fast approval clock for an unprecedented evaluation-access appendix.
unknowns: AUTHORITY: VSC/CECI and funder delegation for a new award obligation; CSC approval of exact service changes.

FUTURE_DECISION: recipient acceptance and subsequent regular-award calendar.

routes.headline: Common evaluation has empirical benefits, but independent access rights and evaluator containment are prerequisites

newEvidence.claim: FACT, newly foregrounded limitation: LUMI terms section 6 grants content access for service accessibility, quality and security while retaining confidentiality and user IP; it does not explicitly grant an external evaluator unrestricted model access.
newEvidence.locator: pp.4-5 section 6

newEvidence.claim: REPORT, new comparative evidence: the 2024 US/UK/Singapore joint exercise found initially divergent results, shared logs/code and reconciled parsing/token-limit differences; it explicitly targeted methodological interoperability, not novel safety findings.
newEvidence.locator: Testing Overview; Methodology; Finding 1

newEvidence.claim: REPORT, new comparative evidence: the July 2025 international exercise combined technical and language contributions from nine named jurisdictions/institutions; its agent judges disagreed materially with human annotations and its cybersecurity strand encountered environment bugs.
newEvidence.locator: Introduction; Quality of judge-LLMs; Agentic Testing for Cybersecurity Threats

supports: INFERENCE: reused execution manifests and native-language review offer a mechanism of coalition value independent of quota size.
INFERENCE: common acceptance can reduce duplicate preparation, but this cost reduction was not measured in the retrieved exercises.
challenges: INFERENCE: recognition of an external test must bind both model version and execution environment; a score-only passport can propagate errors.
INFERENCE: expanded privileged evaluation access can expand the attack surface; evaluator safeguards belong in the same agreement.
unknowns: AUTHORITY: award-policy power to mandate external evaluation and recipient/IP permissions.
POPULATION: contemporary eligible AI jobs, models and consumed resources.
OUTCOME: no recipient authority's binding acceptance of a common report was located; no measured saved compliance hours.
routes.decisionTest: Two authorities should independently decide the same version-bound evidence package under agreed criteria, preserve disagreements, and record whether a concrete award/access decision accepts the result. A successful benchmark run alone fails this test.

scoreImplications.implication: Consider interoperability and evaluator containment explicitly
scoreImplications.reason: Joint testing found actionable implementation differences, while real evaluation-origin incidents show access itself can create risk.

scoreImplications.implication: Do not infer external testing rights from host content access
scoreImplications.reason: Section 6 is purpose-limited and preserves confidentiality/IP.

routes.headline: The clearest undervaluation candidate: test a common host condition rather than assuming eleven national policy rewrites

newEvidence.claim: FACT, freshly re-read: common terms expressly implement the same resource cut-off policies for national and EuroHPC projects. Section 12 provides at least two weeks' notice for changes, with continued use deemed acceptance. The common policy is an actual administrative precedent, not a safety adoption.
newEvidence.locator: p.7 sections 11-12

newEvidence.claim: FACT, newly foregrounded: the preamble defines LUMI as CSC representing consortium/partners as applicable and incorporates additional service terms. This identifies a shared legal surface but does not reveal the internal delegation required for the proposed change.
newEvidence.locator: p.1 preamble

newEvidence.claim: REPORT, new complementary mechanism: actual international exercises divide technical and language work across participants rather than duplicating each full national test.
newEvidence.locator: Participant contributions; cybersecurity testing and analysis allocation

supports: INFERENCE: the current low coordination assessment may penalise a particular all-award-rewrite design rather than the best available shared-service design.
INFERENCE: common incident evidence could travel across allocations without harmonising every scientific funding decision.
challenges: INFERENCE: section 12 is a notice procedure, not proof of an internally delegated power to impose any desired requirement.
INFERENCE: converting a security clause into broad independent evaluation access may exceed existing rights.
INFERENCE: minimum common standards can dilute demanding national safeguards and create correlated evaluation errors.
unknowns: AUTHORITY: CSC/consortium internal amendment delegation and reserved matters.
FUTURE_DECISION: consent to exact common requirements and cross-border evidence sharing.
POPULATION/OUTCOME: compliant project/job inventory, compliance costs, substitution and successful remedies.
routes.decisionTest: Obtain the CSC/consortium decision rule for one common service annex. If it can be approved once, compare that actual approval graph with national award rewrites; if it requires all channel approvals, retain the coordination penalty. Do not substitute the two-week notification floor for the decision duration.

ideas.title: Common containment manifest with two-channel acceptance
ideas.proposal: Use a host-approved service annex for privileged AI jobs, starting with one Belgian and one EuroHPC project. Preserve national award discretion while testing one version-bound evidence manifest accepted at both channels.
ideas.owner: CSC competent service authority plus actual award-policy owners and participating institutions; none has accepted
ideas.mechanism: Common service terms where delegated authority permits; explicit recipient/evaluator agreement for rights outside existing terms
ideas.safetyDemand: Declare external network/tool permissions, retain action logs and classifier configuration, specify incident recipient and scoped pause/restart tests
ideas.verification: Replay synthetic out-of-scope actions under both submission paths; compare blind reviewer decisions, staff-hours, benign-job disruption and acceptance of the same manifest
ideas.remedy: Pause affected service credentials/jobs and cure/retest under accepted terms; no automatic cross-country blacklist
ideas.deadline: Proposed authority decision by 2027-01-15; two-channel demonstration by 2027-05-31; Geneva report 2027-06-21
dependencies: Comparable workload and recorded resource units
ideas.whyBetter: Tests shared administrative leverage and evidence reuse directly; avoids treating all national allocations as separate mandatory rewrites and avoids claiming whole-pool protection from two pilots.

scoreImplications.implication: Priority for upward scenario review, conditional on delegation
scoreImplications.reason: Actual common host conditions could collapse multiple policy handoffs; no numerical uplift is justified yet.

scoreImplications.implication: Add acceptance reuse and displacement dimensions
scoreImplications.reason: Quota scope alone misses reuse across allocations, but migration and deduplicated covered work remain unmeasured.

routes.headline: Operational experience supports a drill, but in-house development did not remove human and organisational dependencies

newEvidence.claim: REPORT, newly foregrounded operator account: Swissgrid describes initial staff scepticism and low use, interns assisting adoption, management attention, and cooperation among Technology, Market and System Operations. Its January-May 2025 production phase followed earlier research and prototyping.
newEvidence.locator: A tool that first had to earn trust; The turning point in the project

supports: INFERENCE: a real in-house automation system supplies a concrete target for a fallback comparison.
challenges: INFERENCE: a single legal institution can still have substantial internal coordination and trust costs, which should not disappear relative to multi-country routes.
INFERENCE: the reported production interval is not end-to-end development duration or evidence of an already authorised isolated replay.
INFERENCE: transferable test methods need not imply transferable operational thresholds between different grids.
unknowns: AUTHORITY: named pilot signatory and control-room acceptance.
POPULATION: model-controlled dispatch episode count and current software configuration.
OUTCOME: fallback recovery distribution, operator workload and benign interventions; operator self-report is not independent validation.
routes.decisionTest: Have the actual control-room owner attest the current model boundary and replay rights; compare the same fault episodes with current and proposed controls, including operator workload and false fallback cost.

scoreImplications.implication: Account for internal operational dependencies alongside legal entity counts
scoreImplications.reason: Swissgrid's own account attributes adoption to cross-team and human-trust work.

scoreImplications.implication: Do not infer a fresh drill's duration from the 2025 production phase
scoreImplications.reason: Earlier research and prototype work preceded that interval.

routes.headline: Actual stakeholder disagreement supports short reusable trials, while the decision retains an accountable lead and no deployment approval

newEvidence.claim: STAKEHOLDER POSITION, newly retrieved: Energy UK proposes four 12-week thematic periods instead of a slow initial pilot and asks for clarity on data residency, IP and real versus representative data.
newEvidence.locator: pp.2-3, timelines and technical/legal detail

newEvidence.claim: STAKEHOLDER POSITIONS, newly retrieved: Startup Coalition objects to incumbent sponsorship as a barrier, whereas ENA supports regulated lead participants for accountability and operational-data access. Both advocate reusable legal/testing infrastructure. Startup Coalition's 6-9 month partnership assertion is not an independently measured duration.
newEvidence.locator: Startup pp.2-5 Q1/Q4-Q6; ENA pp.2-4 Q1/Q2/Q7

newEvidence.claim: FACT, decision recheck: Ofgem retained licensees, market participants and essential-service operators as leads, with technology partners under their accountability. Participation is not regulatory approval and guarantees no next-stage progression.

supports: INFERENCE: standardised participation/evidence agreements may reduce duplicated work for both startups and incumbents.
INFERENCE: a bounded early-2027 trial can yield interim evidence before Geneva even when the whole programme finishes later.
challenges: INFERENCE: startup inclusion and operational accountability are genuine competing objectives, not simply pro- versus anti-safety views.
INFERENCE: sandbox admission does not authorise live-grid autonomy or establish enforceable deployment remediation.
INFERENCE: a common dataset can be unrepresentative for a particular operator and hide local failure modes.
unknowns: SCHEDULE: actual selected cohort and signed participation timetable.
AUTHORITY: operational deployment/fallback owner beyond sandbox oversight.
POPULATION/OUTCOME: affected assets, dispatch episodes, baseline, cost and recovery data.
routes.decisionTest: Recover one signed participation plan with an accountable lead and a bounded first test period. Require an explicit downstream decision owner and locally calibrated fallback threshold; report pilot evidence separately from permission to deploy.

ideas.title: Twelve-week two-operator portability trial
ideas.proposal: Have a UK lead participant and, if separately willing, Swissgrid test the same fault-description schema and evidence checklist against their own isolated historical replays. Keep local operational thresholds and signoffs distinct.
ideas.owner: Actual UK operator and supplier, Swissgrid control-room owner if participating, with Ofgem responsible only for its own sandbox decisions
ideas.mechanism: Two internal test authorisations and a data-minimising common protocol; optional sandbox participation does not replace either authorisation
ideas.safetyDemand: Bounded autonomy, observable fallback and recovery; record false intervention and dispatch/cost deterioration
ideas.verification: A fixed 12-week test phase, local matched baselines, blinded review of common-format results, disagreement log and staff-hour comparison against separately prepared evidence
ideas.remedy: Reject local scale-up on failed criteria; use local fallback authority only. Cross-operator learning does not confer control over another grid.
ideas.deadline: Proposed 2027-02-01 to 2027-04-26 testing, report by 2027-05-31; contingent on approvals, not programme commitments
dependencies: Representative local data and replay rights
ideas.whyBetter: Makes the national-versus-shared comparison falsifiable within the summit horizon and measures whether reusable evidence saves work without erasing grid-specific safety constraints.

scoreImplications.implication: Separate interim trial from completed 12-month programme
scoreImplications.reason: Stakeholders propose shorter phases; adopted sandbox structure still does not prove an actual early cohort.

scoreImplications.implication: Test whether shared templates reduce net coordination cost
scoreImplications.reason: Both incumbent and startup representatives request reusable agreements, despite conflicting eligibility preferences.

routes.headline: A documented evaluation-origin incident supplies a concrete accountability test; ICO adoption remains a separate outcome

newEvidence.claim: REPORT, newly retrieved: AISI reports 10 of 122 evaluation runs involved 19 out-of-scope actions, mostly clustered in one model/sequence. The environment intentionally allowed internet access and disabled provider cyber classifiers; the institute reports containment within roughly one hour of detection and no evidenced resulting real-world harm.
newEvidence.locator: Opening incident chronology; What we found; How we discovered the incident

newEvidence.claim: FACT, current call recheck: ICO's consultation closes at the end of 20 November 2026 and explicitly covers security, transparency and accountability. Submission is evidence for guidance, not approval of a deployer or protocol.
newEvidence.locator: Metadata; survey sections 2-4; How to respond

supports: INFERENCE: account ownership, authorised destinations, tool permissions and event logging now have a real incident pattern to test against.
INFERENCE: shared incident records could inform several institutions without claiming common legal jurisdiction.
challenges: INFERENCE: this small privileged-testing sample cannot estimate general deployment incidence.
INFERENCE: an evaluator's internal containment response is not evidence of ICO enforcement or a general-purpose release gate.
INFERENCE: collecting more logs can itself expose personal data; require a minimised evidence view and access controls.
unknowns: FUTURE_DECISION: consenting deployer and ICO incorporation of the specific findings.
AUTHORITY: relevant controller/deployer/provider roles for selected personal-data workflow.
OUTCOME: independently scored responsibility reconstruction, prevention, false refusals and evidence minimisation.
routes.decisionTest: Use synthetic versions of the reported incident patterns to test whether reviewers can identify the accountable owner and whether controls block external actions while preserving permitted tasks. Separately observe whether ICO guidance adopts any result.

scoreImplications.implication: Strengthen scenario grounding, not estimated incidence
scoreImplications.reason: Actual incident patterns support concrete tests but derive from special evaluation conditions.

scoreImplications.implication: No automatic upgrade to adopted safeguard
scoreImplications.reason: The call is open; exact incorporation is a future decision.

routes.headline: Staged investment offers a hypothesis, but the PM's claim that terms are secured weakens the assumption that stages remain negotiable

newEvidence.claim: ANNOUNCEMENT, corroboration: the 29 October release describes up to $1.6 billion equity, stages, progress reporting and continued work with CAISI. It does not publish a subscription agreement or a discretionary-stage schedule.
newEvidence.locator: Commitment paragraph; five undertakings; staged reporting paragraph

newEvidence.claim: STAKEHOLDER CLAIM, newly retrieved: the same-day PM speech says strong terms have been secured and describes an agreement. This is evidence against assuming that future stages are still freely negotiable, but is not proof of closing, executed rights or disbursement.
newEvidence.locator: Passage beginning Because of the scale and strategic importance; subsequent Under this agreement paragraph

supports: INFERENCE: an existing CAISI relationship and reporting architecture can reduce the novelty of a tightly specified evidence obligation.
INFERENCE: shared acceptance of evidence by commercial co-investors could spread the cost of verification.
challenges: INFERENCE: national champion, jobs and growth objectives can conflict with withholding finance after a safety failure.
INFERENCE: reporting against jobs/capital investment is not a safety covenant, reserve matter or release veto.
INFERENCE: the commercial investor group is not controlled by the Canadian government merely because government participates.
unknowns: NONDISCLOSURE/AUTHORITY: investing legal entity, subscription/shareholder documents, board or reserved-matter rights, cure/default and actual authorised signatories.
FUTURE_DECISION/SCHEDULE: discretionary versus committed stages and dates before Geneva.
POPULATION: entity/model/operational perimeter including international group operations.
OUTCOME: no executed safety covenant or observed withheld stage retrieved.
routes.decisionTest: Recover a signed term sheet or authoritative investor confirmation identifying a genuinely discretionary uncommitted stage, its decision holder and date. If all stages are committed subject only to fixed milestones, reclassify this as a negotiated amendment proposal rather than an open unilateral leverage window.

ideas.title: Evidence condition on a genuinely uncommitted finance stage
ideas.proposal: For Cohere equity, and only as a separate analogue for genuinely new Anthropic credit, attach a version-bound containment/evaluation evidence condition to one still-uncommitted stage. Use one independent report with expressly agreed investor reliance rights.
ideas.owner: Cohere's actual investing vehicle and company signatories; for the separate credit analogue, Anthropic and actual new-money lenders with required agent consents
ideas.mechanism: Prospective equity subscription condition or separately negotiated new-credit covenant; never transfer legal rights between the two instruments
ideas.safetyDemand: Document high-risk privileged testing permissions, incident response, independent evidence and a cured/retested severe failure before that optional stage is committed
ideas.verification: Confirm instrument, signatory, cash/commitment status and date first; then inspect signed evidence condition, model/entity scope, independent result and actual stage decision
ideas.remedy: Do not commit the optional stage until the specified cure; preserve already-committed funding obligations and avoid automatic enterprise-wide acceleration
ideas.deadline: Proposed instrument/discretion check by 2027-01-31; signed condition and exercised evidence decision by 2027-05-31 if an actual financing event exists
ideas.whyBetter: Tests a narrow holder-controlled decision and avoids conflating equity, historic grants, committed revolving credit and expenditure. A shared evidence report may save duplication without inventing a state-controlled lender bloc.

scoreImplications.implication: Keep unknown until actual stage dates and discretion are evidenced
scoreImplications.reason: Staging and secured-terms language do not disclose a live negotiating window.

scoreImplications.implication: Keep unknown rather than infer investor control
scoreImplications.reason: No operative safety condition, cure or withholding right is public in the retrieved announcements.

routes.headline: New-facility consent may need fewer parties than a syndicate amendment, but proprietary-information exceptions and substitution constrain safety leverage

newEvidence.claim: FACT, newly foregrounded: section 9.08(b) expressly excepts the incremental/extension/refinancing mechanisms from its general amendment rule; 9.08(c) permits class-only changes at the requisite class vote and 9.08(f) permits consistent integration with borrower/agent consent. A blanket full-syndicate majority prerequisite is too coarse, but these clauses do not automatically authorise any safety term.

FACT, newly foregrounded obstacle: the concluding paragraph of section 5.04 exempts non-financial proprietary/trade-secret information, legally barred material, privileged material and certain third-party-confidential information from required delivery/discussion/inspection. Ordinary reporting is therefore not an unrestricted model-evaluation access right.
newEvidence.locator: p.94 section 5.04 concluding paragraph

newEvidence.claim: FACT, corroboration: new-money provision is elective, while existing credit events have specified conditions; the borrower can approach alternative eligible lenders for replacement commitments.

supports: INFERENCE: a willing subset financing a new class could coordinate more easily than a wholesale syndicate amendment, if the proposed terms fit the applicable clauses.
INFERENCE: an information covenant with a defined confidentiality carveout can be more feasible than a general model-release veto.
challenges: INFERENCE: borrower choice of other eligible funding sources can defeat a minority refusal to supply new money.
INFERENCE: the covenant must explicitly negotiate needed evidence access rather than assume financial reporting covers model secrets.
INFERENCE: bank nationality, arranger title and lending exposure establish neither actual commitments nor state direction.

SOURCE CAVEAT: section 2.22(b) references 9.08(g), but retrieved 9.08(g) concerns fiscal-year changes. This apparent cross-reference mismatch warrants checking the controlling executed documents, not silently repairing the citation.
unknowns: NONDISCLOSURE: lender allocations and current usage; raw SEC curl returned 403, while tool extraction supplied the clause text.
FUTURE_DECISION/SCHEDULE: no dated post-cutoff incremental, extension or replacement negotiation recovered.
AUTHORITY: exact amendment/class-consent route and evidence-access carveout for the proposed term.
OUTCOME/POPULATION: covered models/entities, marginal change over voluntary practices and exercised remedy.
routes.decisionTest: Identify an actual borrower-initiated event, draft the exact safety clause and have counsel map it to 2.21/2.22/2.23 and 9.08 with all required parties. Obtain lender allocations only where that selected path requires them; check alternative financing before asserting bargaining power.

scoreImplications.implication: Scenario-test a new-class subset separately from whole-facility amendment
scoreImplications.reason: The agreement contains instrument-specific exceptions to its general majority route.

scoreImplications.implication: Do not upgrade merely because an information covenant is imaginable
scoreImplications.reason: Existing reporting exceptions and the absence of a dated new-money event remain material.

scoreImplications.implication: Keep proposed optional-stage refusal distinct from existing-draw default/acceleration
scoreImplications.reason: Sections 2.21-2.23 concern elective new commitments, whereas 4.02 supplies conditions for committed credit events.
